abstract: <jats:p>Stress-inducible promoters are vital for the desirable expression of genes, especially transcription factors, which could otherwise compromise growth and development when constitutively overexpressed in plants. Here, we report on the characterization of the promoter region of a stress-responsive gene SaAsr1 from monocot halophyte cordgrass (Spartina alterniflora). Several cis-acting elements, such as ABRE (ABA-responsive element), DRE-CRT (dehydration responsive-element/C-Repeat), LTRE (low temperature-responsive element), ERE (ethylene-responsive element), LRE (light-responsive element), etc. contributed at varying degrees to salt-, drought- and ABA-enhanced expression of gusA reporter gene in Arabidopsis thaliana under the full-length promoter, pAsr11875 and its deletion derivatives with an assortment of cis-regulatory motifs. The smallest promoter, pAsr1491, with three cis-acting elements (a CCAAT box-heat responsive, an LRE, and a copper responsive element) conferred drought-enhanced expression of gusA; pAsr1755 (with an ABRE and a DRE) presented the highest expression in ABA and drought; and pAsr1994 with seven ABREs and two DREs conferred optimal induction of gusA, especially under drought and ABA. Arabidopsis transgenics expressing a known abiotic stress-responsive gene, SaADF2 (actin depolymerization factor 2), under both pAsr11875 and p35S promoters outperformed the wild type (WT) with enhanced drought and salt tolerance contributed by higher relative water content and membrane stability with no significant difference between pAsr11875:SaADF2 or p35S:SaADF2 lines. However, pAsr11875:SaADF2 lines produced healthy plants with robust shoot systems under salt stress and control compared to slightly stunted growth of the p35S:SaADF2 plants. This reestablished the evidence that transgene expression under a stress-inducible promoter is a better strategy for the genetic manipulation of crops.</jats:p>
title: Characterization of a Stress-Enhanced Promoter from the Grass Halophyte, Spartina alterniflora L.

abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>Glycophyte biomass-derived biochars are currently concerned in most studies. However, little attention is given to the characteristics of halophyte-derived biochars. In this study, five typical halophytes of euhalophytes (<jats:italic>Suaeda altissima</jats:italic>, <jats:italic>Suaeda salsa</jats:italic>, and<jats:italic> Kalidium foliatum</jats:italic>), recretohalophytes (<jats:italic>Phragmites australis</jats:italic>), and pseudohalophytes (<jats:italic>Tamarix chinensis</jats:italic>) which are widely distributed in the arid and semiarid regions of northwestern China were selected for producing biochars with a slow pyrolysis process at 500 °C for 1 h. The harvested biochars were characterized in elemental content, pores, surface area, and surface charges, and then their potential value as a soil conditioner was evaluated. The results showed that the halophyte-derived biochars had variable ash and Na<jats:sup>+</jats:sup> contents, ranging from 7.26 to 23.64% and 1.06 to 33.93 g kg<jats:sup>−1</jats:sup> respectively. The EC value of the biochars ranged from 1.76 to 23.45 mS cm<jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>. The biochar derived from <jats:italic>Suaeda altissima</jats:italic> had a very low specific surface area (SSA), 3.50 m<jats:sup>2</jats:sup> g<jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>, while that derived from <jats:italic>Phragmites australis</jats:italic> (B<jats:sub>PA</jats:sub>) had a very high SSA, 344.02 m<jats:sup>2</jats:sup> g<jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>. All the biochars carried both positive and negative charges. <jats:italic>Kalidium foliatum</jats:italic> biochar (B<jats:sub>KF</jats:sub>) possessed more negative charges, while <jats:italic>Suaeda altissima</jats:italic> biochar (B<jats:sub>SA</jats:sub>) contained more positive charges. In general, the halophyte biochars had a higher ash content and lower point of zero net charge (PZNC) value, compared with the biochars derived from glycophytes, which would imply their higher potential value as an acidic soil conditioner.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>A Gram-negative, aerobic, short rod-shaped bacterium, designated strain YC6898<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>, was isolated from the surface-sterilized root of a halophyte (<jats:italic>Suaeda maritima</jats:italic>) inhabiting tidal flat of Namhae Island, Korea. Strain YC6898<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>grew optimally at 30–37 °C and pH 6.5–7.5. The strain inhibited mycelial growth of<jats:italic>Pythium ultimum</jats:italic>and<jats:italic>Phytophthora capsici</jats:italic>. Phylogenetic analyses based on 16S rRNA gene sequences indicated that strain YC6898<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>belongs to the genus<jats:named-content xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="genus" xlink:type="simple"><jats:ext-link ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="http://dx.doi.org/10.1601/nm.9438" xlink:type="simple"><jats:italic>Hoeflea</jats:italic></jats:ext-link></jats:named-content>in the family<jats:named-content xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="family" xlink:type="simple"><jats:ext-link ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="http://dx.doi.org/10.1601/nm.1398" xlink:type="simple"><jats:italic>Phyllobacteriaceae</jats:italic></jats:ext-link></jats:named-content>. Its closest relatives were<jats:named-content xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="species" xlink:type="simple"><jats:ext-link ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="http://dx.doi.org/10.1601/nm.10253" xlink:type="simple"><jats:italic>Hoeflea alexandrii</jats:italic></jats:ext-link></jats:named-content>AM1V30<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>(96.7 % 16S rRNA gene sequence similarity),<jats:named-content xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="species" xlink:type="simple"><jats:ext-link ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="http://dx.doi.org/10.1601/nm.22560" xlink:type="simple"><jats:italic>Hoeflea anabaenae</jats:italic></jats:ext-link></jats:named-content>WH2K<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>(95.7 %),<jats:named-content xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="species" xlink:type="simple"><jats:ext-link ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="http://dx.doi.org/10.1601/nm.9992" xlink:type="simple"><jats:italic>Hoeflea phototrophica</jats:italic></jats:ext-link></jats:named-content>DFL-43<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>(95.5 %) and<jats:named-content xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="species" xlink:type="simple"><jats:ext-link ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="http://dx.doi.org/10.1601/nm.9437" xlink:type="simple"><jats:italic>Hoeflea marina</jats:italic></jats:ext-link></jats:named-content>LMG 128<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>(94.8 %). Strain YC6898<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>contained Q-10 as the major ubiquinone. The major fatty acids of strain YC6898<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>were C<jats:sub>18 : 1</jats:sub>ω7<jats:italic>c</jats:italic>(61.1 %), C<jats:sub>16 : 0</jats:sub>(11.9 %), 11-methyl C<jats:sub>18 : 1</jats:sub>ω7<jats:italic>c</jats:italic>(9.6 %) and C<jats:sub>19 : 0</jats:sub>cyclo ω8<jats:italic>c</jats:italic>(8.0 %). The polar lipids were phosphatidylcholine, phosphatidylethanolamine, phosphatidylmonomethylethanolamine, phosphatidylglycerol, unknown lipids and an unknown glycolipid. The total genomic DNA G+C content was 53.7 mol%. On the basis of phenotypic, chemotaxonomic and phylogenetic analysis, strain YC6898<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>represents a novel species of the genus<jats:named-content xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="genus" xlink:type="simple"><jats:ext-link ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="http://dx.doi.org/10.1601/nm.9438" xlink:type="simple"><jats:italic>Hoeflea</jats:italic></jats:ext-link></jats:named-content>, for which the name<jats:italic>Hoeflea suaedae</jats:italic>sp. nov. is proposed. The type strain is YC6898<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>( = KACC 14911<jats:sup>T</jats:sup> = NBRC 107700<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>).</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Early changes in physiological and oxidative status induced by salt stress were monitored in two Brassicaceae plants differing in their tolerance to salinity, <jats:italic>Cakile maritima</jats:italic> (halophyte) and <jats:italic>Arabidopsis thaliana</jats:italic> (glycophyte). Growth response and antioxidant defense of <jats:italic>C. maritima</jats:italic> under 400 m<jats:italic>M</jats:italic> NaCl were compared with those of <jats:italic>A. thaliana</jats:italic> exposed to 100 m<jats:italic>M</jats:italic> NaCl. Salinity induced early growth reduction that is less pronounced in <jats:italic>C. maritima</jats:italic> than in <jats:italic>A. thaliana</jats:italic>. Maximum hydrogen peroxide (H<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>O<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>) level occurred in the leaves of both species 4 h after the onset of salt treatment. A rapid decline in H<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>O<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> concentration was observed thereafter in <jats:italic>C. maritima</jats:italic>, whereas it remained high in <jats:italic>A. thaliana</jats:italic>. Correlatively, superoxide dismutase, catalase and peroxidase activities increased at 4 h of treatment in <jats:italic>C. maritima</jats:italic> and decreased thereafter. However, the activity of these enzymes remained higher in treated plants than that in controls, regardless of the duration of treatment, in <jats:italic>A. thaliana</jats:italic>. The concentrations of malondialdehyde (MDA) reached maximum values at 24 h of salt stress in both species. Again, MDA levels decreased later in <jats:italic>C. maritima</jats:italic>, but remained high in <jats:italic>A. thaliana</jats:italic>. The contents of <jats:italic>α</jats:italic>‐tocopherol remained constant during salt stress in <jats:italic>C. maritima</jats:italic> and decreased during the first 24 h of salt stress and then remained low in <jats:italic>A. thaliana</jats:italic>. The results clearly showed that <jats:italic>C. maritima</jats:italic>, in contrast to <jats:italic>A. thaliana</jats:italic>, can rapidly evolve physiological and antioxidant mechanisms to adapt to salt and manage the oxidative stress. This may explain, at least partially, the difference in salt tolerance between halophytes and glycophytes.</jats:p>
title: Early effects of salt stress on the physiological and oxidative status of Cakile maritima (halophyte) and Arabidopsis thaliana (glycophyte)

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p> <jats:bold>
            <jats:italic>Suaeda salsa</jats:italic> L. is a halophytic species that is well adapted to high salinity. In order to understand its salt tolerance mechanism, we examined the growth and vacuolar H<jats:sup>+</jats:sup>‐ATPase (V‐ATPase) response to NaCl within the shoots and roots. The growth of shoots, but not roots, was dramatically stimulated by NaCl. Cl<jats:sup>−</jats:sup> and Na<jats:sup>+</jats:sup> were mainly accumulated in shoots. V‐ATPase activity was significantly increased by NaCl in roots and especially in shoots. Interestingly, antisera ATP95 and ATP88b detected three V<jats:sub>1</jats:sub> subunits (66, 55 and 36 KDa) of V‐ATPase only in shoots, while an 18 kDa V<jats:sub>0</jats:sub> subunit of V‐ATPase was detected by both antisera in shoots and roots. It suggested that the tissue‐specific characteristics of V‐ATPase were related to the different patterns of growth and ion accumulation in shoots and roots of <jats:italic>S. salsa</jats:italic>.</jats:bold> </jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p> <jats:italic>Sarcocornia fruticosa</jats:italic> (L.) A.J. Scott is found in coastal marshes of south‐west Spain, growing under a very wide range of interstitial soil salinity from 10 m<jats:italic>M</jats:italic> up to nearly 1000 m<jats:italic>M</jats:italic>. A glasshouse experiment was designed to investigate the effect of this range of salinities on the morphology and the photosynthetic apparatus of <jats:italic>S. fruticosa</jats:italic> by measuring growth rate, photosynthetic and non‐photosynthetic area, atrophy of distal branch ends, water status, chlorophyll fluorescence parameters, gas exchange and photosynthetic pigment concentrations. The long‐term effects of salinity on the growth of <jats:italic>S. fruticosa</jats:italic> were mainly determined by the extent of photosynthetic area rather than the variations in net photosynthetic rate. Photosynthetic area was reduced at 1030 m<jats:italic>M</jats:italic> as a result of a decrease in the length of the photosynthetic portions. This was induced by fewer internodes and, at salinities lower than 510 m<jats:italic>M</jats:italic>, smaller internode diameter. Net photosynthetic rate increased as the quantum efficiency of photosystem II decreased in the different salinity treatments, which means that the plant could be increasing photorespiration and/or using cyclic electron transport as additional photoprotective mechanisms. The recorded drop in net photosynthetic rate at higher salinities appeared to be due to a reduction in stomatal conductance. The results indicate that <jats:italic>S. fruticosa</jats:italic> is capable of tolerating very high and continued exposure to salt, showing its greatest growth rate at 510 m<jats:italic>M</jats:italic> NaCl.</jats:p>
